plants.name: Rhododendron ponticum
plants.description: Dense domes of bell-shaped, mauve-to-lilac blooms, often with a golden-flecked throat, light up evergreen thickets. In early June the shrubs form soft purple waves across woodland and garden edges.
plants.location: Western Europe, including Ireland and the British Isles, where it is widely grown and naturalised
plants.funFact: Native to Asia Minor and the Black Sea region, it was introduced to Western Europe in the 17th century. It has since spread so vigorously that in parts of Britain and Ireland it is treated as an invasive species.

plants.name: Paeonia lactiflora
plants.description: Lush, ruffled, fragrant blooms open atop glossy, deeply divided foliage. Late-season cultivars such as 'Sarah Bernhardt' unfurl big double pink flowers just as spring gardens turn toward summer.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late spring, typically May to June
plants.location: Temperate gardens of the central United States, such as Missouri, and across the Northern Hemisphere
plants.funFact: The stems die back to the ground each winter, but the plants are long-lived perennials. A well-sited peony can keep flowering in the same spot for decades.

plants.name: Banksia integrifolia
plants.description: Tall, lemon-yellow flower spikes, packed with hundreds of nectar-rich blooms, glow on the windswept dunes and headlands of Australia's east coast. In June, the heart of the Southern Hemisphere winter, they feed honeyeaters and other nectar-loving wildlife.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer through winter, peaking in autumn and still flowering in June
plants.location: Coastal eastern Australia, from Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria
plants.funFact: Each flower spike is made up of hundreds of tiny individual flowers. After they fade, the spike develops into the woody, knobbly seed cone that makes banksias so recognisable.
